claim: The manuscript presents a fully automated high-throughput workflow for 3D-based chemical screening in human midbrain organoids.
source: Here, we present a fully automated workflow in a standard 96-well format that combines generation, maintenance, whole mount immunostaining, tissue clearing, and high-content imaging of automated midbrain organoids (AMOs) (see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated directly in the introduction section of the manuscript.

claim: The workflow uses standard 96-well plates.
source: Here, we present a fully automated workflow in a standard 96-well format that combines generation, maintenance, whole mount immunostaining, tissue clearing, and high-content imaging of automated midbrain organoids (AMOs) (see Figure 1a).
evidence: The text explicitly states the use of standard 96-well format.

claim: AMOs possess a highly homogeneous morphology, size, global gene expression, cellular composition, and structure.
source: The resulting organoids possess a highly homogeneous morphology, size, global gene expression, cellular composition, and structure.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract.

claim: AMOs present significant features of the human midbrain.
source: They present significant features of the human midbrain and display spontaneous aggregate-wide synchronized neural activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: AMOs display spontaneous aggregate-wide synchronized neural activity.
source: They present significant features of the human midbrain and display spontaneous aggregate-wide synchronized neural activity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by calcium imaging and electrophysiology data.

claim: The automated workflow enhances intra- and inter-batch reproducibility.
source: By automating the entire workflow from generation to analysis, we enhance the intra- and inter-batch reproducibility as demonstrated via RNA sequencing and quantitative whole mount high-content imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA sequencing and imaging data.

claim: The workflow allows assessing drug effects at the single-cell level within a complex 3D cell environment.
source: This allows assessing drug effects at the single-cell level within a complex 3D cell environment in a fully automated HTS workflow.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a capability of the system.

claim: AMOs are generated starting from small molecule neural precursor cells (smNPCs).
source: In order to limit cellular heterogeneity during differentiation, we produced human AMOs starting from small molecule neural precursor cells (smNPCs) (Reinhardt et al., 2013a), which in turn originate from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the automation process.

claim: smNPCs originate from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs).
source: In order to limit cellular heterogeneity during differentiation, we produced human AMOs starting from small molecule neural precursor cells (smNPCs) (Reinhardt et al., 2013a), which in turn originate from pluripotent stem cells (PSCs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The workflow omits matrigel embedding to reduce variation.
source: To further reduce batch-to-batch variability, we also omitted matrigel embedding and standardized mechanical stresses by using an automated liquid handling system (ALHS).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a method to reduce variability.

claim: All steps from seeding to analysis are performed in a fully scalable automated fashion using a 96-channel-pipetting head in a robotic ALHS.
source: Starting from seeding the organoids, all following steps including maintenance, fixation, whole mount staining, and clearing are performed in a fully scalable automated fashion using a 96-channel-pipetting head in a robotic ALHS (see Figure 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the automation.

claim: AMOs show little intra- and inter-batch variability in size distribution.
source: The resulting AMOs show little intra- and inter-batch variability in size distribution (see Figure 1b, average coefficient of variation (CV) within one batch 3.56%; min 2.2%, max 5.6%), morphology (see Figure 1c), and cellular composition and organization (see Figure 2), making them ideal for HTS-approaches.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1b showing size measurements.

claim: The average coefficient of variation (CV) within one batch of AMOs is 3.56%.
source: The resulting AMOs show little intra- and inter-batch variability in size distribution (see Figure 1b, average coefficient of variation (CV) within one batch 3.56%; min 2.2%, max 5.6%), morphology (see Figure 1c), and cellular composition and organization (see Figure 2), making them ideal for HTS-approaches.
evidence: This specific value is stated in the Results section.

claim: The workflow generates one aggregate per well.
source: Furthermore, our workflow generates one aggregate per well, maintained independently from others, thus minimizing batch effects due to paracrine signaling observed in bioreactor-based strategies (Quadrato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a feature of the workflow.

claim: The fully automated workflow operates with 99.7% (standard deviation 0.7%) sample retention for automated seeding, aggregation, and maturation steps over 30 days.
source: The fully automated workflow operates with very high efficiency, retaining 99.7% (standard deviation 0.7%) of samples for automated seeding, aggregation, and maturation steps over 30 days and 96.5% (standard deviation 3.1%) of samples for fixation, whole mount staining, clearing, and transfer to flat bottom imaging plates over 12 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 96.5% (standard deviation 3.1%) of samples are retained for fixation, whole mount staining, clearing, and transfer to flat bottom imaging plates over 12 days.
source: The fully automated workflow operates with very high efficiency, retaining 99.7% (standard deviation 0.7%) of samples for automated seeding, aggregation, and maturation steps over 30 days and 96.5% (standard deviation 3.1%) of samples for fixation, whole mount staining, clearing, and transfer to flat bottom imaging plates over 12 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 6.1% (standard deviation 1.3%) of samples are rejected during high-content imaging for presence of dust, damage, or fibers.
source: Lastly, 6.1% (standard deviation 1.3%) of these samples are rejected during high-content imaging for presence of dust, damage, or fibers (see Figure 1d and Supplementary file 1 for source data).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1d.

claim: AMOs express the dopaminergic midbrain marker TH at day 25.
source: Already at day 25, the AMOs contained large numbers of neurons as indicated by the expression of Map2 (Shafit-Zagardo and Kalcheva, 1998) (also see Video 1), β-tubulin III (TUBB3) (Leandro-García et al., 2010) (see Figure 2e), and doublecortin (Gleeson et al., 1999) (DCX, see Figure 2c/d). Presence of high levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, Figure 2a/b, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis (Nagatsu, 1995), as well as the expression of the transcription factors Foxa2, Lmx1a, Nurr1, and Pitx3 (Hegarty et al., 2013) (see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), are consistent with differentiation toward a dopaminergic midbrain fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2a/b.

claim: AMOs express the precursor markers nestin and Sox2 at day 25.
source: Expression of the dopaminergic midbrain marker TH as well as the precursor markers nestin and Sox2 is evenly distributed throughout the entire aggregate at day 25, as shown by single confocal microscopy slices of tissue-cleared samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend and shown in Figure 2a.

claim: AMOs express the transcription factors Foxa2, Lmx1a, Nurr1, and Pitx3, consistent with differentiation toward a dopaminergic midbrain fate.
source: Presence of high levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, Figure 2a/b, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis (Nagatsu, 1995), as well as the expression of the transcription factors Foxa2, Lmx1a, Nurr1, and Pitx3 (Hegarty et al., 2013) (see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), are consistent with differentiation toward a dopaminergic midbrain fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: AMOs contain GABAergic (vGAT) and glutamatergic (vGLUT1) neurons, but their abundance is low compared to dopaminergic neurons.
source: While other neuronal subtypes, specifically GABAergic (vGAT) and glutamatergic (vGLUT1) neurons, are present in AMOs (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1), their abundance is low compared to dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMOs retain a population of neural precursors identified by the expression of Sox2, Brn2, and nestin.
source: As commonly seen in all 3D neural cultures, AMOs retain a population of neural precursors identified by the expression of Sox2 (Ellis et al., 2004) (see Video 1, Figure 2a/b, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), Brn2 (Dominguez et al., 2013; Figure 2c/d and Figure 2—figure supplement 2), and the more general neural marker nestin (Hendrickson et al., 2011) (see Figure 2a/b and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in multiple figures.

claim: AMOs express synapsin, synaptophysin, and homer, indicating the presence of synapses.
source: Expression of synapsin (Thiel, 1993) (see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2) as well as the presynaptic marker synaptophysin and postsynaptic marker homer (Tadokoro et al., 1999) frequently colocalized with each other on Map2-positive neurites (see Figure 2f) and indicated the presence of synapses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: AMOs contain GFAP and S100b double-positive astrocytes at later stages.
source: Consistently, AMOs contained GFAP and S100b double-positive astrocytes (Götz et al., 2015) at later stages (see Figure 2g).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Different cell types within AMOs self-organize into different concentric zones with distinct cellular orientations spanning the entire organoid.
source: We have optimized our AMOs to not form distinct random local subdomains; rather, the different cell types within the AMOs (i.e. neurons, astrocytes, and neural progenitors) self-organize into different concentric zones with distinct cellular orientations spanning the entire organoid (see Figure 2a–c).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2a-c.

claim: The outermost layer of AMOs contains few nuclei with a dense, circumferentially oriented layer of TH+/nestin+/DCX+ cell processes.
source: The outermost layer of the AMOs contains few nuclei with a dense, circumferentially oriented layer of TH+/nestin+/DCX+ cell processes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the zonal organization.

claim: Ultrastructural analysis of AMOs reveals a dense 3D cell architecture consistent with neuronal cell bodies surrounded by nerve fibers.
source: Ultrastructural analysis of AMOs (see Figure 2—figure supplement 3) supported the immunofluorescence data, revealing a dense 3D cell architecture consistent with neuronal cell bodies surrounded by nerve fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Vesicles with the characteristic size and localization of synaptic vesicles are frequently found within nerve fibers of AMOs.
source: Moreover, vesicles with the characteristic size and localization of synaptic vesicles are frequently found within these nerve fibers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing ultrastructural analysis.

claim: qPCR analysis demonstrates increasing expression levels of various neural, midbrain, and glia-specific markers at different developmental stages with concomitant decreases in neural precursor markers.
source: Further quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) analysis demonstrated increasing expression levels of various neural (DCX, Map2, NEFL, NeuN, TBR2, TUBB3, Syt1), midbrain (TH, NURR1, NKX6-1, EN1, GIRK2, AADC), and glia-specific (GLAST, MBP, S100b) markers at different developmental stages with concomitant decreases in neural precursor markers (Brn2, nestin, Pax6, Sox1, Sox2), confirming neural maturation toward a midbrain identity over time (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3.

claim: AMOs show spontaneous, aggregate-wide spikes of calcium activity.
source: In addition to frequent spontaneous activity of individual cells, we observed aggregate-wide synchronous and periodic calcium spikes (see Video 2) in all analyzed AMOs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4 and Video 2.

claim: Calcium activity in AMOs occurs synchronously throughout the entire aggregate.
source: Division of the optical cross-section into quadrants shows that this calcium activity is occurring synchronously throughout the entire aggregate.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 4 legend and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Treatment with cobalt(II) chloride (CoCl2) completely abolished calcium spikes in AMOs.
source: Treatment with cobalt(II) chloride (CoCl2) completely abolished these spikes.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 4 legend and shown in Figure 4g.

claim: MEA measurements revealed spontaneous electrical activity in 35-day-old AMOs.
source: Multielectrode array (MEA) measurements revealed spontaneous electrical activity in 35-day-old AMOs (see Figure 4h/i).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4h/i.

claim: The field potentials of several electrodes in proximity to a 35-day-old AMO oscillated in synchrony over time with two concurrent main frequencies at 1 Hz and 14 Hz.
source: The field potentials of several electrodes in proximity to a 35-day-old AMO (see Figure 4i) oscillated in synchrony over time with two concurrent main frequencies at 1 Hz and 14 Hz (see Figure 4j, upper and lower panels).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4j.

claim: Voltage patch-clamping revealed that cells from AMOs possess typical excitable, neuron-like electrophysiological properties.
source: These typical excitable, neuron-like electrophysiological properties could be detected as early as day 25 (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and in 29 of the 62 recorded cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4l-n.

claim: The average membrane potential of the recorded cells from AMOs was −41.9 ± 15.2 mV (n = 29).
source: The average membrane potential of the recorded cells was −41.9 ± 15.2 mV (n = 29).
evidence: This specific value is stated in the Results section.

claim: AMOs were most similar to the brain and spinal cord in a panel with data from 21 human fetal tissues.
source: Consistent with successful neural differentiation, AMOs were most similar to the brain and spinal cord in a panel with data from 21 human fetal tissues (see Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5a.

claim: On a global gene expression level, AMOs more closely resembled the primary human midbrain samples than published midbrain organoids.
source: On a global gene expression level, AMOs more closely resembled the primary human midbrain samples than published midbrain organoids (AMOs = correlation 0.78, published midbrain organoids = 0.72, see Figure 5b).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5b.

claim: AMOs were consistently more reproducible within and between different batches than current midbrain protocols.
source: This revealed that AMOs were consistently more reproducible within and between different batches than current midbrain protocols, as illustrated by the principal component analysis (PCA) plotted in Figure 5c.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: AMOs from three independently thawed and cultured batches (n = 64 separately processed single organoids in total) clustered much more closely together than the published midbrain organoids (n = 6).
source: The AMOs from three independently thawed and cultured batches (n = 64 separately processed single organoids in total) clustered much more closely together than the published midbrain organoids (n = 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the PCA analysis.

claim: AMOs exhibit no measurable edge effects at the global gene expression level.
source: Importantly, in the PCA plot the AMOs clustered independently of their position on the plate (Figure 5c) and the groups also showed no apparent differences in any of the other analyses (Figure 5a/b), indicating that AMOs exhibit no measurable edge effects at the global gene expression level and further substantiating the high reproducibility of our protocol.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5a-c.

claim: GO analysis of genes significantly upregulated in AMOs compared to published midbrain organoids yielded almost exclusively GO terms connected to neuronal and synaptic activity.
source: This analysis yielded almost exclusively GO terms connected to neuronal and synaptic activity (Figure 5d; for a complete list of GO terms see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The relationship between the amount of tracked cells and measured brightness was highly linear (R2 >0.99) in the optical HTS 3D whole mount analysis workflow.
source: The resulting relationship between the amount of tracked cells and measured brightness was highly linear (R2 >0.99), illustrating the quantitative nature of our optical HTS 3D whole mount analysis workflow.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The comparison of three 96-well plates from independent batches revealed the uniform cellular composition of AMOs within and between independently thawed and cultured batches.
source: The comparison of three 96-well plates from independent batches revealed the uniform cellular composition of AMOs within and between independently thawed and cultured batches (see Figure 6d–g) (Average CVSox2 = 5%, CVMap2 = 9%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6d-g.

claim: The average coefficient of variation for Sox2 in AMOs is 5%.
source: The comparison of three 96-well plates from independent batches revealed the uniform cellular composition of AMOs within and between independently thawed and cultured batches (see Figure 6d–g) (Average CVSox2 = 5%, CVMap2 = 9%).
evidence: This specific value is stated in the Results section.

claim: The average coefficient of variation for Map2 in AMOs is 9%.
source: The comparison of three 96-well plates from independent batches revealed the uniform cellular composition of AMOs within and between independently thawed and cultured batches (see Figure 6d–g) (Average CVSox2 = 5%, CVMap2 = 9%).
evidence: This specific value is stated in the Results section.

claim: Positional analysis detected effects of plate position (edge effects) for Map2 levels but not Sox2 levels with about 10% reduced Map2 brightness of samples in the center of the plate compared with the wells at the edge.
source: Positional analysis detected effects of plate position (edge effects) for Map2 levels but not Sox2 levels with about 10% reduced Map2 brightness of samples in the center of the plate (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) compared with the wells at the edge.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AMOs are more homogeneous with regard to their morphology, cellular structure, size, viability, and protein expression than the automated hiPSC organoids generated from the same cell line and under strictly standardized conditions.
source: In conclusion, AMOs are more homogeneous with regard to their morphology, cellular structure, size, viability, and protein expression than the automated hiPSC organoids generated from the same cell line and under strictly standardized conditions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison.

claim: Three independently cultured batches of automated hiPSC organoids showed up to a 5-fold higher coefficient of variation in cellular viability and up to a 10-fold higher coefficient of variation for organoid size than AMOs.
source: Three independently cultured batches of automated hiPSC organoids showed up to a 5-fold higher coefficient of variation in cellular viability and up to a 10-fold higher coefficient of variation for organoid size than AMOs (see Figure 7g/h, for individual organoid size and viability data see Figure 7e/f).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7e-h.

claim: AMOs respond most strongly to dopaminergic modulation in MEA measurements.
source: Functional responses were consistent with a midbrain identity of AMOs (see Figure 8e/f/g/k). Electric field oscillations of AMOs responded strongly to the addition of modulators of the dopamine pathway, but yielded more limited responses when targeting the GABA pathway (see Figure 8e/f/k).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8e/k.

claim: Automated hiPSC-derived cortical organoids had a weak response to dopaminergic modulation and reacted most strongly to glutamatergic modulation.
source: As expected following cortical differentiation, control hiPSC organoids had a weak response to dopaminergic modulation and reacted most strongly to glutamatergic modulation (see Figure 8h–j,k).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8h-k.

claim: Between 70% and 80% of cells within AMOs are Sox2-negative mature cell types after 30 days of differentiation.
source: Testing AMOs from two separate lines with three independently cultured batches each, we detected between 70% and 80% mature cell types after only 30 days of differentiation with very little variation within and between batches and cell lines (see Figure 8d).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8d.

claim: AMOs spontaneously secrete dopamine into the culture medium at a similar level as found in adult human cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
source: The maturity and dopaminergic midbrain identity of AMOs was further confirmed by the spontaneous and unstimulated secretion of dopamine into the culture medium at a similar level as found in adult human cerebrospinal fluid (CSF, see Figure 8c; Goldstein et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8c.

claim: 6-Hydroxy Dopamine (6OHD) and 1-Methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+) specifically ablate TH-positive dopaminergic neurons from AMOs in a dose-dependent manner.
source: To further assess the physiological relevance of our workflow as well as its ability to quantify drug effects in 3D cell cultures, we treated AMOs from two different cell lines with increasing concentrations of toxins specific for dopaminergic neurons, namely 6-Hydroxy Dopamine (6OHD) and 1-Methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+) (Reinhardt et al., 2013b; Blum et al., 2001; Simola et al., 2007; Meredith and Rademacher, 2011). High-content imaging allowed us to discern distinct effects of these nigral toxins on TH-positive neurons compared to general MAP2-positive neurons in AMOs. While both compounds reduced the number of all neurons in a dose-dependent manner, levels of TH-positive dopaminergic neurons decreased more strongly and at lower concentrations (see Figure 8a/b), with 6OHD having the more specific effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8a/b.

claim: 6OHD has a more specific effect on dopaminergic neurons than MPP+.
source: While both compounds reduced the number of all neurons in a dose-dependent manner, levels of TH-positive dopaminergic neurons decreased more strongly and at lower concentrations (see Figure 8a/b), with 6OHD having the more specific effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the effects of the two toxins.

claim: AMOs show lower variance in cell death/survival in toxicity studies than iPSC-organoids derived from the same cell line.
source: Our automated workflow is compatible with all three types of assay and the results demonstrate that AMOs show lower variance in cell death/survival in toxicity studies than iPSC-organoids derived from the same cell line (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1g, i).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1g, i.

claim: BABB-based clearing proved to be both the fastest and most efficient method in a comparison of different clearing protocols.
source: BABB-based clearing proved to be both the fastest and most efficient method in a comparison of different clearing protocols (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: BABB clearing enables the detection of fluorescent signals like DAPI by confocal microscopy approximately three times deeper in organoids than other clearing protocols.
source: BABB clearing enables the detection of fluorescent signals like DAPI by confocal microscopy approximately three times deeper in organoids than other clearing protocols.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1—figure supplement 1 legend and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Organoids cleared with BABB are significantly less opaque and more permeable to light than those cleared with other protocols.
source: Organoids cleared with BABB are also significantly less opaque and more permeable to light than those cleared with other protocols.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1—figure supplement 1 legend and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The combination of whole mount staining and clearing allows the 3D reconstruction of entire AMOs via confocal imaging.
source: The combination of whole mount staining and clearing allows the 3D reconstruction of entire AMOs via confocal imaging and enables further detailed 3D quantification and analysis, for example tracing of neurites throughout the whole aggregate, which cannot be performed using typical tissue sectioning procedures (see Video 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and demonstrated in Video 1.

claim: The workflow is compatible with manual pipetting and can benefit labs without access to liquid handlers.
source: Importantly, our workflow is also compatible with manual pipetting, and thus can benefit labs without access to liquid handlers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: By starting with neural precursor cells rather than PSCs, the workflow can accelerate and streamline the neural differentiation process.
source: By starting with neural precursor cells rather than PSCs, we can accelerate and streamline the neural differentiation process resulting in highly reproducible, homogeneous, functionally coupled, and electrophysiologically active human 3D microtissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: AMOs do not represent the complexity of the actual human midbrain.
source: While our AMOs do not represent the complexity of the actual human midbrain, we demonstrate the presence of key cell populations with a degree of structure and organization similar to that of other published midbrain organoids (Qian et al., 2016; Jo et al., 2016; Monzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: AMOs' uniformity in key parameters enables large-scale 3D-based HTS strategies.
source: AMOs' uniformity in key parameters such as size, cellular organization, gene expression, and protein levels enables large-scale 3D-based HTS strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The presence of aggregate-wide, reproducible, synchronous calcium and electrical activity in human neural 3D structures may enable neural activity to be used as a HTS-compatible, simple readout for phenotypic screens.
source: Moreover, the presence of aggregate-wide, reproducible, synchronous calcium and electrical activity in human neural 3D structures may enable neural activity to be used as a HTS-compatible, simple readout for phenotypic screens including toxicology studies and drug screening for disorders with altered brain activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a potential application.

claim: None of the available high-throughput-compatible protocols generates midbrain-specific organoids.
source: Importantly, none of the available high-throughput-compatible protocols generates midbrain-specific organoids, but rather they focus on a cortical fate (Sirenko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The model of the human midbrain opens up the potential to perform 3D organoid-based HTS of midbrain-specific disorders including Parkinson's disease.
source: Our model of the human midbrain opens up the potential to perform 3D organoid-based HTS of midbrain-specific disorders including the highly prevalent Parkinson's disease.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a potential application.

claim: The automated whole mount optical analysis can be directly applied to other established 3D protocols.
source: Our automated whole mount optical analysis can also be directly applied to other established 3D protocols and may help uncover phenotypes that manifest themselves primarily in 3D or in distinct subpopulations of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a potential application.

claim: The use of precursor cells as a starting population provides benefits but also sacrifices some of the hiPSCs' broader cell fate potential and complexity.
source: Although the use of precursors cells as a starting population provides benefits, the comparison to hiPSC-based organoids also highlights certain limitations of this approach. Our choice of generating AMOs by seeding more committed neural precursor cells instead of hiPSCs improves the predictability of the differentiation outcome while maintaining the ability to form self-organized tissues. However, it also sacrifices some of the hiPSCs' broader cell fate potential and complexity resulting in simpler structures compared to hiPSC-based organoids.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: smNPCs can only give rise to cells of the ectoderm, which excludes the formation of microglia.
source: In addition, smNPCs can only give rise to cells of the ectoderm, which excludes, for example, the formation of microglia.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: The workflow favors approaches that ectopically add a known number of oligodendrocytes or microglia to AMOs to reach a screenable state much earlier.
source: These long time scales are not very attractive for the design of high-throughput screening strategies. Instead, we favor approaches that ectopically add a known number of oligodendrocytes or microglia to our AMOs and thus reach a screenable state much earlier.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposed solution.

claim: AMOs fill the gap between heterogeneous PSC-derived organoids and established but less physiological spheroid- and 2D-based screening formats.
source: AMOs fill the gap between heterogeneous PSC-derived organoids and established but less physiological spheroid- and 2D-based screening formats.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: The workflow is a contribution to help translate successful strategies such as cell painting and other big-data-generating high-content strategies into biologically relevant 3D models.
source: Therefore, we see our workflow as a contribution to help others translate successful strategies such as cell painting (Bray et al., 2016) and other big-data-generating high-content strategies (Friese et al., 2019; Scheeder et al., 2018) into biologically relevant 3D models.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: 9000 smNPCs were seeded in each well of a conical 96-well plate in smNPC medium to generate AMOs.
source: After digestion by accutase, we seeded 9000 smNPCs in each well of a conical 96-well plate (Thermo Fisher) in smNPC medium and allowed them to aggregate for 2 days.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing AMO generation.

claim: 0.4% (w/v) polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) was added to increase inter-cell adhesion during AMO generation.
source: To increase inter-cell adhesion, we added 0.4% (w/v) polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, Sigma-Aldrich).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing AMO generation.

claim: Organoids were fed every other day for the entire duration of culture.
source: Organoids were fed every other day for the entire duration of culture.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing AMO generation.

claim: The workflow adapted an extended 3D-staining protocol and combined it with benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate (BABB)-based tissue clearing.
source: In order to characterize protein localization in our AMOs (>600 μm diameter) and assess the efficiency of their neural/midbrain differentiation at a cellular resolution and in a HTS-compatible manner, we adapted an extended 3D-staining protocol (Lee et al., 2016) and combined it with benzyl alcohol and benzyl benzoate (BABB)-based tissue clearing (Dent et al., 1989).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the staining and clearing workflow.

claim: AMOs were stained with primary and secondary antibodies for 6 days each.
source: After fixation with 4% PFA (VWR) for 10–15 min, we stained the aggregates with primary and secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor secondary antibodies, Thermo Fisher) for 6 days each.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing whole mount staining and clearing.

claim: Between primary and secondary antibody incubation as well as after the staining procedure, samples were washed 5 times for 1 hr with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS.
source: Between primary and secondary antibody incubation as well as after the staining procedure we washed the samples 5 times for 1 hr with 0.1% Triton X-100 in PBS.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing whole mount staining and clearing.

claim: The extremely long staining procedure allows the antibodies to fully penetrate the aggregates despite their large size and high density.
source: This extremely long staining procedure allows the antibodies to fully penetrate the aggregates despite their large size and high density.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a rationale for the protocol.

claim: Samples were dehydrated stepwise through a methanol series (25%, 50%, 70%, 90%, 100%, 15 min each) for BABB clearing.
source: First, the samples were dehydrated stepwise through a methanol (Roth) series (25%, 50%, 70%, 90%, 100%, 15 min each).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing whole mount staining and clearing.

claim: Samples were incubated for 30 min in 1:1 methanol/BABB and subsequently kept in BABB for imaging.
source: The samples were incubated for 30 min in 1:1 methanol/BABB (benzyl benzoate (Sigma-Aldrich) and benzyl alcohol (Sigma-Aldrich) 1:1) and subsequently kept in BABB for imaging.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing whole mount staining and clearing.

claim: Image acquisition was carried out in an Operetta high content imager (Perkin Elmer).
source: Image acquisition was carried out in an Operetta high content imager (Perkin Elmer) and images were analyzed in Harmony 4.1 software and/or Columbus version 2.6.0.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing high-content imaging.

claim: Images were analyzed in Harmony 4.1 software and/or Columbus version 2.6.0.
source: Image acquisition was carried out in an Operetta high content imager (Perkin Elmer) and images were analyzed in Harmony 4.1 software and/or Columbus version 2.6.0.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing high-content imaging.

claim: A total of 16 confocal planes in three channels (DAPI, Sox2 488 nm, and MAP2 647 nm) with an inter-plane spacing of 36.6 μm were acquired for a total stack of 549 μm.
source: We acquired a total of 16 confocal planes in three channels (DAPI, Sox2 488 nm, and MAP2 647 nm) with an inter-plane spacing of 36.6 μm for a total stack of 549 μm, covering the entire aggregate height (clearing and dehydration steps tend to shrink and flatten aggregates slightly).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the detailed high-content imaging analysis example.

claim: All RNA sequencing data generated was deposited to the NCBI GEO database (GSE119060).
source: All RNA sequencing data generated by us was deposited to the NCBI GEO database (GSE119060) and can be accessed at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE119060.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Parkinson's disease affects 2–3% of the population aged 65 and above.
source: One structure of particular interest in the context of disease modeling and drug development is the midbrain due to its role in the highly prevalent Parkinson's disease (affecting 2–3% of the population aged 65 and above Poewe et al., 2017) and many other developmental disorders (Barkovich, 2012; Doherty et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) is the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis.
source: Presence of high levels of tyrosine hydroxylase (TH, Figure 2a/b, also see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), the rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine synthesis (Nagatsu, 1995), as well as the expression of the transcription factors Foxa2, Lmx1a, Nurr1, and Pitx3 (Hegarty et al., 2013) (see Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), are consistent with differentiation toward a dopaminergic midbrain fate.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Gliogenesis follows neurogenesis in vivo.
source: Since gliogenesis follows neurogenesis in vivo (Miller and Gauthier, 2007), we expected the emergence of astrocytes after the initial formation of neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: In the cortex, neurons form cortical layers with distinct markers.
source: In the cortex, neurons form cortical layers with distinct markers. Cortical 3D models recapitulate this layer organization to a degree (Lancaster et al., 2013; Paşca et al., 2015; Qian et al., 2016; Mariani et al., 2015; Bhaduri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The midbrain does not possess the typical layer organization of the cortex.
source: In contrast, the midbrain does not possess the typical layer organization of the cortex, hence published midbrain organoids are devoid of cortex-like layers (Qian et al., 2016; Monzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Published midbrain organoids are devoid of cortex-like layers.
source: In contrast, the midbrain does not possess the typical layer organization of the cortex, hence published midbrain organoids are devoid of cortex-like layers (Qian et al., 2016; Monzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Typical published midbrain organoids initially form random local subdomains of organized tissue within the bulk of the organoid, often in the form of rosettes.
source: Due to their self-organizing nature, typical published midbrain organoids initially form random local subdomains of organized tissue within the bulk of the organoid, often in the form of rosettes (Jo et al., 2016), a hallmark of the very early stages of neural development (Perrier et al., 2004; Elkabetz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Rosettes are a hallmark of the very early stages of neural development.
source: Due to their self-organizing nature, typical published midbrain organoids initially form random local subdomains of organized tissue within the bulk of the organoid, often in the form of rosettes (Jo et al., 2016), a hallmark of the very early stages of neural development (Perrier et al., 2004; Elkabetz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Large-scale synchronous bursting behavior can be observed in several developing brain regions in vivo.
source: Large-scale synchronous bursting behavior can also be observed in several developing brain regions in vivo (Ben-Ari, 2001) and in brain slices in vitro (Silva et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: Large-scale synchronous bursting behavior can be observed in brain slices in vitro.
source: Large-scale synchronous bursting behavior can also be observed in several developing brain regions in vivo (Ben-Ari, 2001) and in brain slices in vitro (Silva et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The workflow used a Beckman Coulter Biomek FXP liquid handling station equipped with a 96-channel-pipetting head and an attached Cytomat incubator.
source: All liquid handling steps (seeding, maintenance, and fixation of organoids) were performed by a Beckman Coulter Biomek FXP liquid handling station equipped with a 96-channel-pipetting head and an attached Cytomat incubator (Thermo Fisher).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing AMO generation.

claim: The workflow used a Dragonfly spinning disc confocal microscope (Andor, Oxford Instruments) for calcium imaging.
source: Imaging was performed using a Dragonfly spinning disc confocal microscope (Andor, Oxford Instruments) at a frequency of 10 Hz for 4 min.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing calcium imaging.

claim: Electrophysiological measurements on microelectrode arrays were performed on electrode areas of 9-well MEAs.
source: Electrophysiological measurements on microelectrode arrays (USB-MEA256system, Multichannel Systems) were performed on electrode areas of 9-well MEAs as previously described (Piccini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing electrophysiological analysis by MEA.

claim: The workflow used an EPC-10 amplifier (HEKA Elektronik) and Patchmaster acquisition software (HEKA Elektronik) for patch-clamping.
source: Recordings were done using an EPC-10 amplifier (HEKA Elektronik) and Patchmaster acquisition software (HEKA Elektronik).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing electrophysiological analysis by patch-clamping.

claim: RNA sequencing reads were aligned to the human genome hg19 with TopHat2 aligner (v2.1.1).
source: We aligned the RNA sequencing reads to the human genome hg19 with TopHat2 aligner (v2.1.1) (Kim et al., 2013), using default input parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Gene annotation from Ensembl (version GRCh37.87) were used in the mapping process.
source: Gene annotation from Ensembl (version GRCh37.87) were used in the mapping process.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The number of reads that were mapped to each gene was counted using the Python package HTSeq (v0.7.2).
source: The number of reads that were mapped to each gene was counted using the Python package HTSeq (v0.7.2) (Anders et al., 2015) with 'htseq-count – mode union – stranded no'.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: RPKM values for each gene were computed by Cufflinks (v2.2.1).
source: RPKM values (Reads Per Kilobase of transcript per Million mapped reads) for each gene were computed by Cufflinks (v2.2.1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: PCA and differential expression analysis were performed with raw counts using the R package DESeq2 (v1.18.1).
source: PCA and differential expression analysis were performed with raw counts using the R package DESeq2 (v1.18.1).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Genes were considered as deregulated if |log2FC| > 2 and FDR < 0.05 using Benjamini-Hochberge multiple test adjustment.
source: Genes were considered as deregulated if |log2FC| > 2 and FDR < 0.05 using Benjamini-Hochberge multiple test adjustment (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment was analyzed with the bioinformatics web server Gorilla and visualized with REViGO.
source: Gene Ontology (GO) term enrichment was analyzed with the bioinformatics web server Gorilla (Eden et al., 2009) and visualized with REViGO (Supek et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing RNA sequencing analysis.

claim: The workflow used the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay (Promega) to measure the viability of individual organoids.
source: To measure the viability of individual organoids we used the CellTiter-Glo 3D Cell Viability Assay (Promega) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing the organoid viability assay.

claim: The workflow used a Dopamine ELISA Kit (Abnova) to measure dopamine secretion.
source: We collected the cell culture supernatant from 35 days old organoids 40 hr after feeding and measured its dopamine content using a Dopamine ELISA Kit (Abnova) according to the manufacturer's instructions.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section describing dopamine secretion measurement.

claim: The workflow can accommodate several aggregates per well if paracrine signaling is desired.
source: If paracrine signaling is desired, our workflow can easily accommodate several aggregates per well.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a flexibility of the workflow.

claim: The workflow minimizes batch effects due to paracrine signaling observed in bioreactor-based strategies.
source: Furthermore, our workflow generates one aggregate per well, maintained independently from others, thus minimizing batch effects due to paracrine signaling observed in bioreactor-based strategies (Quadrato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The workflow abolishes the need for labor-intensive tissue sections.
source: Moreover, our combined whole mount immunostaining and clearing workflow abolishes the need for labor-intensive tissue sections and allows for quantitative whole mount high-content analysis of entire organoids with single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section.

claim: The workflow allows for quantitative whole mount high-content analysis of entire organoids with single-cell resolution.
source: Moreover, our combined whole mount immunostaining and clearing workflow abolishes the need for labor-intensive tissue sections and allows for quantitative whole mount high-content analysis of entire organoids with single-cell resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section.

claim: The automation of the entire workflow from seeding to analysis in standard plates allows for easy scale-up and implementation into existing screening facilities.
source: Our automation of the entire workflow from seeding to analysis in standard plates allows for easy scale-up and implementation into existing screening facilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Introduction section.

claim: The workflow is designed for automation and allows the quantification of entire dense, large-scale aggregates (>800 μm diameter) with single-cell resolution and high sensitivity.
source: In contrast, our workflow is custom-tailored for automation and allows the quantification of entire dense, large-scale aggregates (>800 μm diameter) with single-cell resolution and high sensitivity, as highlighted by a dose-response assay for 3D cellular detection (see Figure 6a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The homogeneity of AMOs allows extrapolation of data even from single medial confocal slices, drastically shortening acquisition times.
source: In the context of HTS-compatibility, this homogeneity is advantageous, as this trait allows us to extrapolate data even from single medial confocal slices, drastically shortening acquisition times (see Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The workflow used a standard 96-well format along with optimized protocols providing full compatibility with standard liquid handlers in most screening facilities.
source: In designing our workflow, we used a standard 96-well format along with optimized protocols providing full compatibility with standard liquid handlers in most screening facilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow omits cumbersome matrix embedding steps to eradicate variation originating from positional differences of cells within extracellular matrix (ECM) droplets during embedding.
source: By omitting cumbersome matrix embedding steps, we eradicate variation originating from positional differences of cells within extracellular matrix (ECM) droplets during embedding.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow can benefit labs without access to liquid handlers as it is compatible with manual pipetting.
source: Importantly, our workflow is also compatible with manual pipetting, and thus can benefit labs without access to liquid handlers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow results in highly reproducible, homogeneous, functionally coupled, and electrophysiologically active human 3D microtissues.
source: By starting with neural precursor cells rather than PSCs, we can accelerate and streamline the neural differentiation process resulting in highly reproducible, homogeneous, functionally coupled, and electrophysiologically active human 3D microtissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow demonstrates the presence of key cell populations with a degree of structure and organization similar to that of other published midbrain organoids.
source: While our AMOs do not represent the complexity of the actual human midbrain, we demonstrate the presence of key cell populations with a degree of structure and organization similar to that of other published midbrain organoids (Qian et al., 2016; Jo et al., 2016; Monzel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow may help uncover phenotypes that manifest themselves primarily in 3D or in distinct subpopulations of cells.
source: Our automated whole mount optical analysis can also be directly applied to other established 3D protocols and may help uncover phenotypes that manifest themselves primarily in 3D or in distinct subpopulations of cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The neural precursor-based proof-of-principle may be suitable for screens for diseases affecting primarily neural precursors including Zika virus infection.
source: The neural precursor-based proof-of-principle demonstrated here may be suitable, for example, in screens for diseases affecting primarily neural precursors including Zika virus infection. While this condition has been intensively studied using organoids, platform technologies for 3D high-throughput screens are still lacking and in high demand (Qian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Platform technologies for 3D high-throughput screens for Zika virus infection are still lacking and in high demand.
source: While this condition has been intensively studied using organoids, platform technologies for 3D high-throughput screens are still lacking and in high demand (Qian et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow adapted cortical organoids by Paşca et al., 2015/Sloan et al., 2018 to be scaled-up and analyzed in the system as automated hiPSC-based control organoids.
source: Furthermore, other non-midbrain organoid protocols may benefit from our workflow; for example, we have adapted cortical organoids by Paşca et al., 2015/Sloan et al., 2018 to be scaled-up and analyzed in our system as automated hiPSC-based control organoids for our midbrain model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Automation of the existing manual cortical organoid protocol necessitated some modifications.
source: Automation of this existing manual protocol necessitated some modifications (summarized in Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The workflow used accutase-digested single cell suspensions originating from feeder-free iPSC-cultures rather than dispase-treated colonies lifted off partially or whole from feeder-based iPSC-cultures.
source: For example, in order to create a workflow that is as scalable and as repeatable as possible, we decided to use accutase-digested single cell suspensions originating from feeder-free iPSC-cultures rather than dispase-treated colonies lifted off partially or whole from feeder-based iPSC-cultures.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a modification to the original protocol.

claim: The use of colonies as a starting point makes colony/aggregate sizes difficult to control, especially in an automated setting.
source: The use of colonies as a starting point makes colony/aggregate sizes difficult to control, especially in an automated setting, resulting in a variable starting point for each organoid generated in this fashion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a rationale for the modification.

claim: The workflow aggregated and maintained the resulting organoids in SBS-compatible U-bottom plates that facilitate automated handling of all organoids as separate biological replicates.
source: We also aggregated and maintained the resulting organoids in SBS-compatible U-bottom plates that facilitate automated handling of all organoids as separate biological replicates, each in its own well, rather than in 100 mm dishes as in the original publication.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a modification to the original protocol.

claim: The modifications to the original cortical organoid protocol may have changed the outcome compared to the published original.
source: These modifications to the original protocol may have changed the outcome compared to the published original; however, we demonstrate proper forebrain differentiation at the RNA and protein levels, and provide detailed single organoid-based high-content data from three independent batches for select parameters.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section acknowledging a limitation.

claim: The modifications provide the most rigorous comparison between iPSC- and precursor-based organoid approaches by starting both protocols with well-defined and easily controllable cell numbers as single cell suspensions.
source: We also believe that these modifications provide the most rigorous comparison between iPSC- and precursor-based organoid approaches by starting both protocols with well-defined and easily controllable cell numbers as single cell suspensions.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a rationale for the modifications.

claim: Mechanical standardization alone cannot compensate for the innate variability of PSCs during their self-organization.
source: Despite our efforts to standardize iPSC-based organoids in a modified automated workflow, AMOs displayed a distinctly lower variance in a broad set of parameters, including size, cellular subpopulations, and survival in toxicity studies. This may indicate that mechanical standardization alone cannot compensate for the innate variability of PSCs during their self-organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The choice of generating AMOs by seeding more committed neural precursor cells instead of hiPSCs improves the predictability of the differentiation outcome while maintaining the ability to form self-organized tissues.
source: Our choice of generating AMOs by seeding more committed neural precursor cells instead of hiPSCs improves the predictability of the differentiation outcome while maintaining the ability to form self-organized tissues.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The choice of generating AMOs by seeding more committed neural precursor cells sacrifices some of the hiPSCs' broader cell fate potential and complexity resulting in simpler structures compared to hiPSC-based organoids.
source: However, it also sacrifices some of the hiPSCs' broader cell fate potential and complexity resulting in simpler structures compared to hiPSC-based organoids.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: smNPCs are capable of efficiently generating oligodendrocytes.
source: Although smNPCs are capable of efficiently generating oligodendrocytes (Reinhardt et al., 2013a; Ehrlich et al., 2017), they generally arise very late in neural development (Goldman and Kuypers, 2015), and other organoid protocols also demonstrate the presence of oligodendrocytes after 100 days of differentiation or more (Marton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Oligodendrocytes generally arise very late in neural development.
source: Although smNPCs are capable of efficiently generating oligodendrocytes (Reinhardt et al., 2013a; Ehrlich et al., 2017), they generally arise very late in neural development (Goldman and Kuypers, 2015), and other organoid protocols also demonstrate the presence of oligodendrocytes after 100 days of differentiation or more (Marton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Other organoid protocols demonstrate the presence of oligodendrocytes after 100 days of differentiation or more.
source: Although smNPCs are capable of efficiently generating oligodendrocytes (Reinhardt et al., 2013a; Ehrlich et al., 2017), they generally arise very late in neural development (Goldman and Kuypers, 2015), and other organoid protocols also demonstrate the presence of oligodendrocytes after 100 days of differentiation or more (Marton et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Long time scales for oligodendrocyte emergence are not very attractive for the design of high-throughput screening strategies.
source: These long time scales are not very attractive for the design of high-throughput screening strategies.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Similar strategies for the introduction of microglia into hiPSC-based neural organoids have recently been described, albeit without the ability to perform HTS.
source: Similar strategies have recently been described for the introduction of microglia into hiPSC-based neural organoids (Lin et al., 2018; Abud et al., 2017; Muffat et al., 2018), albeit without the ability to perform HTS.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The emerging science of 3D cell culture promises to probe the effects of drugs on single cell types in an intact niche as part of a complex 3D in vitro culture.
source: The emerging science of 3D cell culture promises to probe the effects of drugs on single cell types (here: dopaminergic neurons) in an intact niche as part of a complex 3D in vitro culture.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Understanding the effects in context will be an essential factor to better understand biology at the tissue level.
source: Understanding the effects in context will be an essential factor to better understand biology at the tissue level.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: 3D cell culture science is in a phase of transition, where traditional manual low throughput protocols need to be adapted to unbiased higher throughput workflows.
source: Currently, 3D cell culture science is in a phase of transition, where traditional manual low throughput protocols need to be adapted to unbiased higher throughput workflows.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: Adapting traditional manual low throughput protocols to unbiased higher throughput workflows is a prerequisite to mine the information necessary to merge organoid science with the promises of big data and machine learning.
source: This is a prerequisite to mine the information necessary to merge organoid science with the promises of big data and machine learning to better tackle the complexities of understanding 3D biology.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow is a contribution to help translate successful strategies such as cell painting and other big-data-generating high-content strategies into biologically relevant 3D models.
source: Therefore, we see our workflow as a contribution to help others translate successful strategies such as cell painting (Bray et al., 2016) and other big-data-generating high-content strategies (Friese et al., 2019; Scheeder et al., 2018) into biologically relevant 3D models.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: The workflow can contribute to establishing a next generation of cellular 3D in vitro disease models that allow unbiased, quantitative, high-throughput access to human tissue-surrogates in a dish.
source: Taken together, we hope that our automation approach can contribute to establishing a next generation of cellular 3D in vitro disease models that allow unbiased, quantitative, high-throughput access to human tissue-surrogates in a dish.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a concluding statement.
